notes.meaning: Jesus kept traveling and teaching in Galilee, the northern region. He stayed away from Judea because the leaders there wanted to kill Him after He healed a man on the Sabbath (John 5). He was not acting out of fear. He was being wise, because His time to die had not yet come.

The Feast of Tabernacles was a happy week-long festival in the fall. Families lived in shelters made of branches to remember how God cared for Israel in the wilderness. It also thanked God for the harvest. It was one of three feasts every Jewish man was expected to attend in Jerusalem.

Jesus' brothers pushed Him to leave quiet Galilee and go to Judea, where crowds would see His miracles. It sounded like friendly advice. But it was really bossy, and probably mocking. They hoped He would make a big name for Himself.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Church teaches that Mary stayed a virgin all her life. So it understands these 'brothers' as other close relatives, since Hebrew speakers often called any relative a 'brother.'

notes.meaning: The brothers thought Jesus must want fame, like anyone else. So why hide in small villages? 'Show Yourself to the world,' they said. People expected the Messiah, God's promised king, to appear in some dazzling way. But Jesus' true glory would be shown on the cross.

John explains that even Jesus' own family did not trust Him as the Messiah. Being related to Jesus did not save them. Faith in Him is what counts. Later, after the resurrection, His brothers did come to believe (Acts 1:14).

Jesus answered them gently. He lived by His Father's timing, and the right moment had not yet come. For His brothers, any time would do, because nothing big depended on when they went. It is a reminder to wait for God's time rather than set it ourselves.

Here 'the world' means people living without God. It could not hate the brothers, because they fit right in with it. It hated Jesus because He told the truth that its deeds were evil. People who speak honestly against sin can expect the same push-back.

Jesus told His brothers to go on to the feast without Him. He was not going just now, because His time had not fully come. He was not lying, since He went later (v. 10). He meant He would not go now, and not in the public way they wanted.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Old handwritten copies differ here. Some say 'I am not going up' and others say 'I am not yet going up.' Scholars weigh the evidence differently, but most agree there is no real contradiction with verse 10.

notes.meaning: Jesus stayed in Galilee for a few more days. He would not let others' advice push Him around. He kept steady to His own plan.

After His brothers left, Jesus also went to Jerusalem. He went quietly, not with the big crowds of travelers. He was avoiding a fuss and trouble with the leaders, not tricking anyone. Once He arrived, He taught openly.

'The Jews' here means the religious leaders, not the whole people. They kept looking for Jesus at the feast, and not for any good reason. Their question 'Where is He?' had a scornful ring, like 'Where is that fellow?'

People in the crowds whispered and argued about Jesus. Some called Him a good man. That was true, but it fell short of the whole truth, since He is the Son of God. Others said He was fooling people. Jesus divides people. No one can stay neutral about Him.
No one dared to speak openly about Jesus, because they feared the leaders. The rulers wanted His name hushed up and forgotten. Fear had silenced the people.

About halfway through the eight-day feast, Jesus went into the temple courts and began to teach. He had avoided a grand arrival. But once there, He boldly did the teaching that the priests should have been doing.

The leaders were amazed. Jesus had never studied under a famous rabbi (a Jewish teacher), yet He knew and explained the Scriptures better than anyone. Instead of being moved, many used this as a reason to look down on Him.

Jesus said His teaching did not come from human schools or from His own ideas. It came from God the Father, who sent Him. He spoke like an ambassador who carries his king's message. So His words carry God's own authority.

Here is a promise for anyone. If you truly want to do what God wants, you will come to know whether Jesus' teaching is from God. An honest, willing heart is the key to understanding. God gives light to those ready to obey.

Jesus gives a simple test of a true teacher: who gets the glory? Someone speaking only for himself wants praise for himself. Jesus sought honor for the Father who sent Him. That shows He is true and not a fake.
The leaders were proud of having God's law from Moses. Yet they did not keep it. Plotting to kill Jesus broke that very law. So they were the real law-breakers, not Him.

Many in the crowd were visitors who did not know about the leaders' plot. They thought Jesus was imagining things. 'You have a demon' meant 'You're out of your mind!' Jesus did not answer the insult, a model of patience for us.

Jesus pointed back to one miracle: healing the disabled man at the pool of Bethesda on the Sabbath (John 5). People were shocked and upset mainly because He did it on the day of rest. That healing was why the leaders wanted Him dead.

Circumcision was a small cutting ceremony for baby boys. It was a sign of God's covenant, His binding promise to His people. It began with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, long before Moses. The law said it must be done on the eighth day, so the Jews did it even when that day fell on the Sabbath.
Jesus' point was simple. If you can treat one small part of a baby on the Sabbath, surely I can heal a whole man on the Sabbath. Acts of mercy fit the true purpose of God's day of rest.

Jesus told them to stop judging by how things look on the surface. Instead, they should judge fairly, by what God's law really means. They also misjudged Jesus Himself, because He looked so ordinary. We should judge people by what is true, not by appearances.
Unlike the visitors, people who lived in Jerusalem knew the leaders wanted Jesus dead. So they were surprised to see Him teaching in the open.

Jesus spoke boldly, and no one stopped Him. Some wondered, maybe half joking, whether the rulers had secretly decided He was the Christ, God's promised king. The real reason was that God was holding back Jesus' enemies until His time came.
